candidates.text:
the path to obsidian was direct only in that: i did not want it to lead to obsidian.

i refuse to believe i need anything heavier than textedit. apple notes is a stretch. it's not about being beholden to the apple kingdom. though i do not love that. that's not the thing for me

i'm not a wordcel. i'm a discount shape rotator. i don't get overattached to text. the only way i can put anything down on purpose is by not looking at it.

i quite literally mean not looking at it. when i type with the intention of writing i don't look at the words, i slightly zoom out my eyes and peripherally look down at the keypad like the little letters popping up are strange alien fish swimming through the thick distorted safety glass of an aquarium. does it sound stupid. yes it sounds insane. does it work. also yes.

i work append only. there is no backwards there is only forwards.

when i was like 10 years old i was elite at looking at words i put on screen and not nitpicking them out of existence. it's a pretty hard skill that comes easily to a kid and it must be practiced to keep it. i do not practice it. i decided to be bad at it.

you can choose to be good at something. why can't you choose to be bad at something?

of course it's because people are choosing this all the time. and not admitting it to themselves.

but i admitted it to myself. i had no delusions of grandeur. i knew my notes were going nowhere. so i did not indulge in elaborate knowledge management systems.

i was wrong. maybe. we'll see together. first i'm telling you the ways i was right.

these apps all have a bias toward inaction. they're aspirational.

i don't feel good saying that. it's not pretty.

humans want to make things. it kind of gives me some sort of existential pain. when i think about all the things we do to fool ourselves like we're making a thing instead of just making the thing.

husband was once talking to the child and he pointed to some tall buildings out a window and he said, look. only humans make things. when you get big, you have to make things too.

the child said, like money?

husband said, like money. or big tables made of stone

i'm a capitalist, ok? but we're it.

we are the things that make things.

there's many research papers on how housekeepers have the highest job satisfaction. cleaning is so concrete. it's dirty, bad and then clean, good. the reward function is constant, you see the progress as it happens.

ok. but knowledge workers aren't obsessively cleaning. then why? why are they obsessively cleaning gardening filing normalizing data in knowledge management apps?

there's another research paper on housekeepers. this one's different.

it's about hotel housekeepers. the hotel housekeepers were asked if they get any exercise and all mostly reported no, none. then they told half the housekeepers that, actually, cleaning is exercising and is in fact easily over and above the recommended daily exercising. a month later, that half of the housekeepers now perceived themselves as getting lots of exercise. and, in that same month later, with nothing else changed, their bodies changed. lower weight, lower blood pressure, lower whatever they were measuring. nothing changed except being told their work counts as working out.

ok. where am i going with this? first it proves me right and then it proves me wrong.

i sort of think these apps make us like markdown housekeepers.

we've been told markdown housekeeping is like the intellectual equivalent of working out. or something. whatever. the thing that will lead to what we humans wish for. which is to make things.

but the housekeeping of it all tricks us into thinking that it's the acting on it. that's not the acting on it you want. there's no credit for well manicured note lawns.

the goal of taking notes is to finish an essay. or a short story or a book or a post or whatever it is you're writing towards. you have to do the thing that gets you final credit. you can't just collect notes on 700 things forever.

so we're doing all the housekeeping and none of the making and our bodies of work are not changing.

our aspiration is not housekeeping.

husband is disciplined. i don't even want to talk about how disciplined he is, it makes me sick. discipline is when you do the thing even when you don't want to it and you do it when you said you were going to do it.

i appear disciplined. it's not that i'm not, i am. i do have discipline. but what i have more of is grit. once i get started, i will solve til the death of it. i'm an object in motion that stays in motion. once i get in motion.

this has always been true of me. i've hacked myself in a million ways to surreptitiously siphon off ambient latent motion.

one way i do that is not cleaning up at night. i do the dishwasher, because that's a strict dependency. otherwise i go to sleep. i leave everything undone.

i get up in the morning and i'm immediately accosted. by undoneness. the morning light is harshest to the dog hair on the dark wood floors. there's couch blankets unfolded. throw pillows everywhere. probably some on the floor. probably in all the dog hair.

i do not see all this and think, ugh. i see all of it and i think: wins. look at all these easy fucking wins.

i worked with a founder and i told him this story. he said, holy shit. i do that too.

he said, for him, he sees it like a steve jobs thing. every couch blanket folded or throw pillow chopped is a tiny insignificant dent on the universe to start the day. to get him in motion.

he said, it's his way of waking up and proving to himself he's not in a simulation. now he can go out into the day, and try for making more significant dents.

you see where i was wrong right?

long story not short, i'd been stuck on a problem and i finally disambiguated the one stupid thing i needed to disambiguate and as soon as i pulled the right thread all of it unraveled easily into done.

obsidian became obvious.

sort of.

the reason it worked is not like, i discovered lots of secret gems hidden in my notes. i did not mindmap myself.

the reason is i had a nice mess to clean up. i do daily dated notes in apple notes and it's been 6,986 days since the iphone first shipped.

i used the ais to convert everything to normalize everything to codify everything. now the nice mess was still a mess but more like a nice pile.

i imported it into obsidian, set up a base to track status changes, and told a friend i made a plan to process at least 100 notes at the end of every weekend.

she was like. BAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAH

she said, no way. it'll just take one day with one too many coffees and you'll level it all.

it was saturday and that day of leveling was sunday.

i am totally uninterested in giving advice. i'm allergic to having a message. i'm only going to tell you what i see, now, about myself:

obsidian is a case study in letting the system emerge.

obsidian is the reward. it is not the forcing function. it is the reward for having forced myself to function.

one way i force myself to function in getting something done is to sentence myself to something i want to do less.

it's W34 of 2026 and i'm still writing in W27. i haven't swept anything out of W27, into my system of scratchpads, because every time, as i'm about to do some thankless sweeping, i keep seeing a thing in there. i so do not want to do the sweeping that suddenly that thing, that bad unfinished worthless thing looks good and ready and then i sneak it onto its own page and suddenly i've sat down and written the whole thing.

i sat down to fold some blankets and chop some pillows and now i've written more words in 2 months than i have in 24.

there's good advice from people who give great advice and it says do something for 100 days. i'm saying for me, i should have said fuck it. i did it for at least 6,986 days and i think maybe i only needed to do it for 10.

i overestimated how little motion i need to become an object in motion that stays in motion.

the prescription of time is like the misdirection from the magician. the magic trick is you killing your disgust reflex. you're snuffing out your aversion.

your aversion is to the narcissism of it all. of documenting everything you do and think and read and watch. everything you experience, you must react to, and note and document. it's so important. i'm so important. my opinions are so important. i must be documented. someone's going to find this like leonardo's diaries and they'll see the brilliance.

but i realized that all of that is true. it is a narcissistic pursuit but i've come to appreciate that the narcissist's narcissistic pursuits have great value.

it kills me to write this. i think the narcissism is actually healthy.

is there some more flattering way to say it? i don't know if i had a healthy enough amount of narcissism. the narcissistic outputting bestows you the benefit of having a minimum critical mass of your own material to work with.

that's why duration of time did not matter. the only part that mattered is i did not allow myself to put other people's shit in there. the impulse to save other people's work is my aversion to narcissism. i did not let myself save links and quotes. i told myself if i need them i'll find them again.

i must process it. that does not mean i process it like it's some expensive cut of steak. i am not coveting and salting and tenderizing and dry aging and searing. i am processing. i process it like it's sausage. i let it be poor quality and floppy and gross like a raw hot dog is. it's fine that i'm repulsed by what i put down. but i must put it down.

the point is i made a mess but it's my mess and the reward is i got to take the mess and move it into obsidian and clean it. now i have a mess that's mine and it's all mine, gloriously mine. i am not stewarding some fan garden of other people's makings. it's my shit. it has existential weight.

bearing existential weight is what it means to make something

candidates.text:
LA LAKERS DEAL: IT’S NOT A LOOPHOLE

Bill Veeck bought the Cleveland Indians in 1946 and popularized the structure now being called a billionaire tax dodge.

His argument was simple.

A sports franchise is not merely a name and a league membership. 

It is a portfolio of player contracts. 

Those contracts are wasting assets: players age, contracts expire, and rosters turn over. 

Wasting assets can be written off over their useful lives.

Players age. 

(LeBron James remains under active investigation by our best scientists.)

Veeck amortized the value of his roster.

The IRS fought variations of it for decades. 

But courts repeatedly accepted the underlying principle: player contracts have finite economic lives and therefore meet the standard for amortization.

Congress did not miss a beat. Congress addressed this several three times.

In 1976, Congress created a presumption that no more than 50% of a franchise’s purchase price should be allocated to player contracts unless the buyer could justify more. 

That was a guardrail, not a prohibition.

In 1993, Congress enacted Section 197—the modern 15-year amortization rule for purchased goodwill and other business intangibles—but specifically excluded professional sports franchises.

Then, in 2004, Congress reversed course. 

The American Jobs Creation Act repealed the exclusion and brought sports franchises under Section 197 alongside other businesses that acquire goodwill, trademarks, customer relationships, and similar intangible assets.

The 2004 law made the write-off slower, not faster.

The reason takes a minute to explain, but it is the whole story.

When you buy a business, you do not buy 'a business' for tax purposes. 

You buy a basket of assets. 

The purchase price must be divided among those assets, and each category may have a different cost-recovery schedule.

Before 2004, a dollar allocated to player contracts could generate deductions over roughly five years. 

A dollar allocated to franchise value or goodwill generally produced no annual amortization deduction.

Its basis might be recovered at sale, but not along the way.

Same dollar out the door. Wildly different tax outcome. Everything depended on which line of the appraisal captured it.

Buyers therefore had an enormous incentive to allocate as much of the purchase price as possible to the roster. 

Franchise sales became appraisal battles over how much value belonged (i) to the players vs. (ii) the franchise name itself.

When Bud Selig’s group bought the Seattle Pilots and moved them to Milwaukee, it allocated $10.2 million of the $10.8 million purchase price to player contracts—roughly 94%. The franchise itself was assigned just $500,000.

In effect, the buyers argued that the team was worth about six cents on the dollar without its players.

The court upheld the allocation.

Congress's 2004 law largely ended that fight. 

Player contracts, franchise rights, trademarks, and goodwill acquired with a team generally became amortizable over the same 15-year period.

Buyers gave up the possibility of writing off aggressive roster allocations over five years. 

In exchange, they gained the ability to amortize the broader pool of acquired intangible value over fifteen.

The rule became simpler. No need to bucket the purchase across players vs franchise'

The deductions became slower but broader.

You can argue that fifteen years is too short. 

So, this is not an accidental gap that clever lawyers discovered between two paragraphs of the tax code.

That is not a gap in the text.

That is the text.

candidates.text:
The best comp is Wise. 

Applied for a national trust bank charter. Presents some obvious money laundering risks. Received the OCC’s decision on its charter application this summer.

The key difference is that with Wise, the OCC scrutinized the company holistically, rather than just looking at the proposed Wise National Trust (WNT) bank. All the Wise baggage was considered because, as the OCC wrote in its rejection, “WNT would be a small aspect of a larger enterprise with a purpose to enable the continued growth and scale of Wise.”

Tellingly, this same approach was not taken with World Liberty. The OCC did not consider the risks or questions raised by commenters about World Liberty Financial (of which there are many) in its evaluation of World Liberty Trust’s application because, “World Liberty Financial, Inc., is not a party to this application.” This despite the fact that World Liberty Trust’s purpose is obviously to enable the continued growth and scale of World Liberty Financial.

If I worked at the OCC, or Wise, or any company that is currently regulated by the OCC, or any company that is considering applying for a bank charter from the OCC, I would find this inconsistency disturbing.
